summary.text: The maiden moulded of earth at Zeus's command — the price of stolen fire, a beautiful evil named Pandora because all the Olympians gave her a gift; from her comes the race of women, and from her jar the ills that walk silent among mankind.
The first woman fashioned by the gods; her daughter by Epimetheus is Pyrrha.
Her birth was carved in relief on the pedestal of the Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon — Hesiod and others, Pausanias notes, having sung that she was the first woman.
Moulded from clay by Vulcan at Jove's command and given a soul by Minerva; each god gave a gift, whence the name; she was given in marriage to Epimetheus, and bore Pyrrha.

story.text: She is Zeus's answer to the stolen fire — the price of the flame, a beautiful evil made as its price. At his command the famous Lame God moulded from earth the likeness of a modest maiden, and the goddess bright-eyed Athena girded and clothed her in silvery raiment and crowned her with a golden crown that the Lame God wrought himself. In the Theogony she has no name at all: she is simply the maiden, sheer guile not to be withstood by men — and from her is descended the race and tribe of women.

In the Works and Days the gods each add their portion. Hephaestus mixes earth with water and puts in it the voice and strength of human kind; Athena teaches her needlework and the weaving of the varied web; golden Aphrodite sheds grace and cruel longing about her head; the Charites and queenly Persuasion hang golden necklaces on her, the rich-haired Hours crown her with spring flowers; and Hermes the Argus-Slayer contrives in her breast lies and crafty words and a deceitful nature. He names her Pandora — All-gift — because all they who dwelt on Olympus gave each a gift, a plague to men who eat bread; and then he leads her to Epimetheus, who forgets his brother's warning and takes her in.

Then the woman took the great lid off the jar with her hands and scattered all that was within, and her thought caused sorrow and mischief to men — for before that day the tribes of men had lived on earth remote and free from ills and hard toil and the heavy sicknesses. Only Hope remained inside in her unbreakable home under the rim of the great jar, for by the will of Zeus the lid caught her before she could fly out. It is a jar, a pithos, in Hesiod — and of these seven sources only Hesiod tells of it; the famous box belongs to her later afterlife, not to any ancient teller.

Hyginus reshapes the workshop. In his telling Prometheus, son of Iapetus, first fashioned men from clay; then Vulcan, at Jove's command, made from clay the form of a woman, and it was Minerva who gave it a soul — in Hesiod the breath of life is Hephaestus' commission and Athena merely dresses the finished maiden. The other gods each gave her some gift, and for that they named her Pandora. She was given in marriage to Epimetheus, and her daughter was Pyrrha — and of the jar Hyginus says not a word.

To the later tradition she is simply the beginning of humankind's female half. Apollodorus, pausing on the flood, calls Pyrrha the daughter of Epimetheus and of Pandora, 'the first woman fashioned by the gods'; and Pausanias, standing before the gold-and-ivory Athena in the Parthenon, records that on the pedestal of the statue is wrought in relief the birth of Pandora — of whom Hesiod and others have sung that she was the first woman, and before her womankind did not yet exist.
Hesiod moulds her from earth at the gods' command with no named polis; Epimetheus receives her as the universal first woman — residence stays deferred.
